summary: Explains problems with IPv6 site-local unicast addresses in their original form and formally deprecates them. Existing use may continue until a replacement is standardized and implemented, but new work should not rely on them.

plainLanguage.summary: One kind of IPv6 address meant for use inside one site caused confusion, so this document says to stop using it for new things.

questions: why were ipv6 site local addresses deprecated
what replaced ipv6 site local addresses
can i still use site local addresses
subtitle: Why IPv6 site-local addresses (FEC0::/10) were retired, and what that does and does not stop.

tldr.problem: IPv6 site-local addresses were meant to be private to one site, but the same address can exist in many sites and nobody agrees on what a site is. That hurt application developers, network managers and router builders.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists these problems and formally deprecates the site-local prefix FEC0::/10. New implementations must stop supporting its special behavior, while existing deployments may keep using it.
tldr.outcome: The prefix may not be reassigned except by a future IETF standards action, and routers should block it by default. An address scheme without ambiguity is pointed to as the better alternative.

facts.label: New implementations
facts.value: MUST NOT support the special behavior

facts.label: Reassignment
facts.value: Only by a future IETF standards action

facts.label: Existing deployments
facts.value: MAY continue to use the prefix

today: RFC 3879 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The site-local prefix FEC0::/10 it deprecated is therefore still marked deprecated by this document, which also points to the Unique Local IPv6 Unicast Addresses work as an example of an unambiguous alternative.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
Site-local addresses are a kind of IPv6 unicast address defined in the IPv6 addressing architecture (RFC 3513, section 2.5.6). They were meant to be usable only inside one site. The IPv6 working group debated their problems for some time. It reached a measure of agreement in March 2003 that the problems were serious enough to replace them in their original form, and confirmed in July 2003 the need to document the issues and deprecate the addresses. The RFC admits the consensus was far from unanimous.

The document describes the adverse effects of site-local addresses, then formally deprecates them. Companion documents are expected to describe the goals of a replacement and specify one. In the meantime the formal deprecation lets existing usage continue until the replacement is standardized and implemented.
sections.plainLanguage: People argued about a certain kind of private address for a long time. This note writes down why it caused trouble and says not to build new things on it.

sections.title: The Ambiguity Problem for Developers
sections.content:
The root defect is ambiguity. An address such as FEC0::1 can exist in several sites at once, and the address itself says nothing about which site it belongs to. That is hard on applications, especially on multi-homed hosts (connected to several sites at once) and mobile hosts (connected to different sites over time).

An application that remembers a correspondent as FEC0::1234:5678:9ABC and tries to connect will fail unless it also supplies a site identifier, written like FEC0::1234:5678:9ABC%1. The identifier can differ from one host instantiation to the next (sometimes %1, sometimes %2), so it cannot be stored or learned from a name server. Developers found this management hard to understand and hard to carry out.

Applications that share IP addresses in their payloads have a second problem. They must decide which addresses may be passed across site boundaries, which in practice means learning something about the network topology. Using a site-local address across sites can give unexpected errors such as a connection reset by peer, or a connection to the wrong node. Multi-party applications are hardest, since a node cannot know where the addresses it hands out will eventually be sent. Using only global addresses would avoid this but would shut such applications out of isolated or intermittently connected networks that only have site-local addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: If two schools both have a Room 1, you must always say which school you mean. Programs kept forgetting to do that, and the numbering of schools changed from day to day.

sections.title: Leaks and Network Management
sections.content:
The RFC compares site-local addresses to the private addresses of RFC 1918 in IPv4 networks. In theory such addresses stay local. In practice they leak: names and literal addresses of private hosts show up in mail messages, web pages and files, and private addresses end up as the source or destination of TCP and UDP traffic, for example in DNS or trace-route requests. Such requests fail, or the response arrives at unsuspecting hosts. Private addresses also get used as targets of reverse DNS queries, uselessly loading the DNS infrastructure.

The RFC calls the leakage largely unavoidable. Some protocols are intrinsically scoped (it names Router Advertisement and Neighbor Discovery), but most applications have no concept of scope and no way to express it. Because the addresses are ambiguous, a network manager cannot easily tell who caused a leak, so leaks are hard to fix.
sections.plainLanguage: Notes meant to stay inside one school keep falling out of backpacks and landing in other schools. Because every school has a Room 1, nobody can tell which school the note came from.

sections.title: Router Complexity
sections.content:
In theory, a site is contiguous and its routers can treat site-local addresses as unambiguous. In practice, large networks get partitioned, so sites become disjoint. Site-local packets then need to cross an intermediate network such as a backbone, which leads to heavy use of tunneling, multi-sited routers, or both.

A multi-sited router breaks the classic rule that the exit interface depends only on the destination address and a single routing table. For site-local packets the route depends on the interface the packet arrived on. Interfaces must be tied to sites, and routing entries become site-dependent. That needs special provisions in routing protocols and the table virtualization techniques normally used for VPNs. Site border routers must also filter, so that packets with a site-local source never leave the site, and that filtering interacts with forwarding. The RFC notes that sites could be built from existing constructs such as domains and areas, but the factors that set site boundaries differ from those that set domain and area boundaries, which adds management complexity.
sections.plainLanguage: A mail sorter who handles several schools must keep a different list for each school, and must remember which door the letter came in through. That is a lot more work than one list.

sections.title: Why 'Site' Is Ill-Defined
sections.content:
The scope model assumes concentric scopes: a host is on a link, the link is in a site, and the site is in the Internet. The RFC argues that experts have argued about what a site is for years without consensus, which suggests there is none to find. Apart from link-local, scope boundaries are ill-defined. Is a whole corporate network a site, or only one geographic location? Does a firewalled DMZ belong to the same site as the internal hosts?

Depending on whom you ask, a site boundary might mean a security, reachability, routing, QOS, administrative or funding boundary, or some combination. Scope-breaking phenomena such as intermittently connected networks, mobile nodes and networks, inter-domain VPNs, hosted networks, and network merges and splits mean scopes overlap and extend into one another, and the scope relationship between two hosts may even differ per protocol. The RFC concludes that the concept of site is naive and does not map operational requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Ask ten people where one school ends and the next begins and you get ten answers. The playground, the bus and the after-school club do not fit neat circles.

sections.title: Toward a Better Alternative
sections.content:
The RFC acknowledges that site-local addresses have perceived benefits: they are simple, stable and private. It argues the same benefits can come from an alternative architecture in which addresses are not ambiguous and carry no simple explicit scope. It cites the Hinden/Haberman work on Unique Local IPv6 Unicast Addresses, which was a Work in Progress at the time.

  • Developers: unambiguous addresses remove the need to manage site identifiers. Applications can treat them like global addresses, though some pain remains because the addresses will not always be reachable.
  • Managers: leaks are not eliminated, but they become much simpler to debug.
  • Routers: standard routing techniques work and no per-interface tables are needed. Border routers still must filter some source ranges, which is a fairly common function.
  • Scope itself: dropping explicit scope removes the problems of defining a site. Non-reachability can be obtained with firewalls.

Anycast addresses remain an open question, because they are ambiguous by construction. The RFC says link-local or global anycast addresses can be baked into code and that further study is needed on anycast with scope between link-local and global.
sections.plainLanguage: The fix is to give every room a number that is unique across the whole world. Then 'meet in room 8431' always means one place, and a front-door guard can still keep strangers out.

sections.title: The Deprecation and IANA Action
sections.content:
The RFC formally deprecates the IPv6 site-local unicast prefix defined in RFC 3513, 1111111011 in binary or FEC0::/10. The requirements are:

  • The special behavior of the prefix MUST no longer be supported in new implementations.
  • The prefix MUST NOT be reassigned for other use except by a future IETF standards action.
  • Router implementations SHOULD be configured to prevent routing of the prefix by default.
  • Existing implementations and deployments MAY continue to use the prefix.

References to site-local addresses should be removed as soon as practical from the revisions of Default Address Selection (RFC 3484), the Basic Socket Interface Extensions for IPv6 (RFC 3493) and the addressing architecture (RFC 3513). Incidental references should be removed from other documents when they are updated, and the RFC lists RFC 2772, RFC 2894, RFC 3082, RFC 3111, RFC 3142, RFC 3177 and RFC 3316 as examples. IANA is asked to mark FEC0::/10 as 'deprecated', pointing to this document.
sections.plainLanguage: New things must not use the old numbering. Old things may keep using it for now. The numbers are locked away so nobody can reuse them without a big official decision.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says ambiguous site-local addresses can hurt network security through leaks, ambiguity and potential misrouting, so removing ambiguity helps with many of those problems.

On the other side, the site-local prefix lets firewall rules and address selection rules block traffic, which is commonly viewed as a security feature because it keeps packets from crossing administrative boundaries. The RFC points out that such blocking rules can be configured for any prefix, including the expected future replacement. If those rules are actually enforced, deprecating the site-local prefix does not endanger security.
sections.plainLanguage: Mixed-up room numbers can send people to the wrong place. A guard at the door can block visitors no matter what numbering you use, as long as the guard really does the job.

viz.caption: THE FIVE PAINS DESCRIBED IN SECTION 2

items.title: Scope identifiers
items.text: Applications must supply a site identifier such as %1, which varies by host.

items.title: Local addresses
items.text: Passing addresses across sites causes errors or connections to the wrong node.

items.title: Leaks
items.text: Private addresses escape in mail, web pages, files and DNS traffic.

items.title: Router complexity
items.text: Multi-sited routers need site-dependent routing, like VPN table virtualization.

items.title: Ill-defined site
items.text: No agreed definition of a site, and scopes overlap in practice.
